overall_summary: Analysis of deduplicated observations clearly shows that 'What If' scenarios and extreme planetary science topics published within the last 3 weeks are heavily outperforming older psychological, historical, or biological facts. Videos involving immersive existential danger or extreme cosmic environments (e.g., Venus, liquid diamond planets, dark planets, and burning ice worlds) generate significantly higher velocity, likes-per-view, and engagement than standard static trivia.

winning_patterns.evidence: Videos like 'What If You Fell Into a Liquid Diamond Planet?' (1,029 views, 38 likes) and 'What If You Fell Into the Planet of Burning Ice?' (972 views, 18 likes) dramatically outperform static fact listings.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on hypothetical immersion formats ('What If You Fell Into...') focusing on extreme physics and exotic extraterrestrial destinations.

winning_patterns.evidence: Titles featuring counterintuitive cosmic truths like 'Venus Has a Day Longer Than Its Year' (981 views) and 'The Planet Darker Than Coal' (1,030 views) gain high sustained traffic.
winning_patterns.action: Continue sourcing bizarre, highly specific astronomical phenomena with high cognitive dissonance.

weak_patterns.evidence: Topics like 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' and 'The Psychological Trick to Stop Songs Stuck in Your Head' stagnate below 60-70 views after weeks of exposure.
weak_patterns.action: Deprioritize psychological trivia and standard human biology facts unless framed as extreme survival or sci-fi scenarios.

weak_patterns.pattern: Short-form historical mysteries without visual scale
weak_patterns.evidence: 'The 2,000-Year-Old Mystery Science Can't Solve' fails to generate the same velocity as cosmic disaster or planetary exploration hooks.
weak_patterns.action: Shift historical storytelling strictly toward high-stakes cinematic scenarios or micro-dramas rather than abstract museum-style trivia.
